generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, reference lists are full of journal articles, so the pattern you use most adds the article title, the journal name, the volume, the issue and the page range to the author and year. Different subjects lean on different sources: a biomechanist cites lab journals, a coach cites coaching-science articles, a management student cites policy reports. The order of elements is fixed, so once you know the pattern you can build an accurate reference for a study, a report or a web page without guessing.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students reference the same coaching-science journal article in their essays.

Tom copies the reference straight from the library database: OKAFOR, Blessing. Small-Sided Games And Decision Making In Youth Football. 2021. Journal of Sports Coaching. The elements are mostly there, but the order and formatting are wrong. The first name is spelled out, the article title is over-capitalised, the year sits in the wrong place, and the volume, issue and page range are missing. This is what copying from a database often produces.

Amara builds the reference by hand from the pattern: Okafor, B. (2021) 'Small-sided games and decision making in youth football', Journal of Sports Coaching, 12(3), pp. 40-55. Surname then initial, year in brackets, article title, journal name, volume and issue, then pages. It is accurate, consistent, and ready for an alphabetical list.

Both students had the same article. Only Amara's reference would pass a marker's eye.
generatedProse.summary: A sport reference is built from a fixed set of elements in a set order. A journal article adds the article title, journal name, volume, issue and page range to the author and year. Build each reference yourself from the pattern, rather than trusting a database to do it, and check it before it goes in your list. The next lesson is about the style that sets these patterns, and applying it consistently across your work.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reference accurate where Tom's was not?

items.text: It followed the fixed order and formatting: surname then initial, year, article title, journal, volume, issue and pages.
It was copied more carefully from the same database.
It used more of the author's full name and more capital letters.
It left out the volume and pages to keep the entry short.

feedback.correct: That's right. Building from the pattern kept every element in the right place.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Compare how each reference handled the order and formatting of the elements.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's reference was accurate because it followed the fixed order and formatting, built by hand rather than copied from the database.
